1. Validate the current bill: confirm meter reads imply 786 kWh (60,886 − 60,100), line items sum to $150.65 ($18.79 + $27.33 + $104.53), and the change versus last month is −$8.20 ($150.65 − $158.85); treat any arithmetic mismatch as a suspected billing error.

2. Map each billing period to its AEP Ohio tariff: last month (2026-03-11 to 2026-04-10, 874 kWh) falls entirely under the pre-2026-04-10 tariff (fixed $18.38; variable $0.0263125 + $0.13441 = $0.1607225/kWh). The current period (2026-04-10 to 2026-05-10, 786 kWh) begins exactly on the new tariff’s effective date, so it falls entirely under the new tariff (fixed $18.788; variable $0.0347738 + $0.13299 = $0.1677638/kWh); no proration is needed because the boundary aligns with the period start.

3. Set days_usd = 0 because both periods are 30 days.

4. Estimate weather_usd from NOAA degree days: compare last month (CDD 15.5 / HDD 444.5) to current (CDD 42 / HDD 215), derive a weather-to-kWh coefficient from the bill history, convert the weather-driven kWh difference to dollars at the effective rate, or set weather_usd = 0 if no defensible coefficient can be estimated.

5. Compute price_usd from the tariff changes (higher fixed charge and higher blended variable rate) applied to baseline usage; compute usage_usd from the 88 kWh decrease (874 → 786) valued at the effective rate; set usage_usd as the residual so price_usd + days_usd + weather_usd + usage_usd equals exactly −$8.20.

6. Check for a billing error by comparing the tariff-modeled current-period total to the actual $150.65; if the difference exceeds rounding, set billing_error_suspected = true and billing_error_usd to the discrepancy, otherwise false and null.

7. Return only the JSON object with keys price_usd, days_usd, weather_usd, usage_usd, billing_error_suspected, and billing_error_usd.
